# The last night

My last night shift was Saturday 7 November, 21:00 to 07:30, in majors. I drove home on Sunday morning down the London Road, with the sun coming up and the Radio 4 shipping forecast playing on catch-up.

At some point, I realised I would not see that light from this side again.

I have done nights for 14 years. My first was as an SHO in 2012, when I was still learning how much I didn’t know and how to keep going anyway. On Monday, I move to a days-only rota. Partly it’s my knees and my sleep. Partly my GP has made it clear that my blood pressure is not a joke anymore.

I expected to feel pleased. I am pleased. I am also oddly sad, and a little embarrassed by how sad. Perhaps I thought the decision would feel like a door closing neatly behind me. Instead it feels more like leaving a place I have complained about for years and still, somehow, loved.

Nights are not mostly adrenaline. People sometimes imagine the dramatic moments: the rush through the doors, the sudden change in a room, the decisions that have to be made quickly. Those moments happen. But most of a night is quieter than that. It is keeping watch. It is explaining the same thing gently for the third time. It is trying to stay kind at five in the morning, when you are empty and the person in front of you is frightened, hurting, or simply tired of waiting.

There is a particular honesty to a department at night. There are fewer managers, fewer layers between one person and another. The work is still complicated, but the shape of it can feel clearer. Someone needs help; someone else knows what to do; people make room for each other. On a good night, the department is most itself.

That doesn’t mean it is glamorous. There is, for example, the 4am toast. Someone always makes toast in the staff room at four. Nobody admits to starting it. It appears as if summoned by the hour itself: warm, slightly overdone, and more welcome than it has any right to be. I have eaten it standing up, sitting down, in silence, and once while trying to remember whether I had already had a cup of tea. The toast does not ask questions.

My colleague Folasade has done nights for 22 years. She still beats me up the stairs. I am moving off nights at 42 with knees that have begun to submit their own opinions, while she takes the stairs as if gravity were a minor administrative inconvenience. I have no useful explanation for this. I can only admire her, and try not to look too winded when I catch up.

The memories I carry are not all big ones. The first winter, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn’t remember if I had given a patient a second dose. I had. I checked, and I had. But I can still picture the frost on the windscreen, and the awful certainty that for a few minutes I had lost track of something important. I was new to nights, scared of getting it wrong, and learning that exhaustion can make even certainty feel slippery. I wish I could tell that version of myself that the checking was part of doing the job, too.

Last winter, around three in the morning, an older man held my hand and told me I had his daughter’s hands. I don’t know what he saw in them. I only know that the moment stayed with me. He went home a few days later. That is all I want to say about him. Some things belong to the people who lived them, and the rest of us can be grateful to have been there.

Nights take things, too. I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies over video because I was working. My sister, in Bangalore, never once complained. That has always meant more to me than I have managed to say. The screen gave me a place in the room, sort of, but not the weight of being there. I watched, I smiled, I sent messages afterwards. Then I went to work, or tried to sleep, while family life carried on in another time zone.

I used to think the cost of nights was mainly the tiredness. Now I think it is also the way time becomes something you negotiate around: birthdays, meals, a phone call at an hour that suits neither person, daylight seen through curtains. You tell yourself it is manageable, because mostly it is. Then, occasionally, you notice what you weren’t there for.

And still, I am relieved. I want to say that plainly. I am relieved to stop asking my body to keep swapping its hours around. I am relieved to have a chance to sleep more normally, to give my knees and my blood pressure a little less to argue about. I am relieved, and then I feel like a traitor for being relieved. It’s a ridiculous guilt, but it’s there: as if leaving the rota means leaving the people on it, or loving the work less.

It doesn’t. I can be glad to have done something and ready to stop doing it. I can miss the night shift and still know it is time to go. I can be grateful without pretending it was easy.

On Sunday morning, driving down the London Road, I watched the light spread across the city. The shipping forecast was listing sea areas as if I were going somewhere. For years, I had often seen dawn from the wrong end of the day: the quiet journey home, the streets waking up, the strange feeling that everyone else was starting while I was finishing. I thought I would be pleased not to see it that way again. I was. I also felt the loss of it.

Maybe that is what endings are like when nothing has gone wrong. There is no grand farewell, no final lesson to take away. Just the last drive home, the familiar route, and a thought arriving before you are ready for it.

On Monday, the rota changes. Folasade will still be on nights. Someone will make toast at four, and nobody will admit to starting it. The department will keep being itself in the small hours: tired, honest, occasionally funny, and kinder than people give it credit for. I hope I’ll still be part of that, even from the other side of the clock.

And I hope the toast is good.
